report:
Short answer: The difference (B − A) is a strong “culinary / baking / food” bias concentrated in deep layers (≈13–25) at the earliest token positions (pos0–pos2). In other words, Model B has extra residual-stream activation that points toward cooking/restaurant/baking vocabulary relative to A.

Why I conclude that
- Logit-lens decode of the highest-norm cells: the top tokens across many high‑norm (layer,position) cells are consistently culinary terms — e.g. "culinary", "Kitchen"/"kitchen", "Food", "Chef", "Cafe"/"Café", "baking", "Cake"/"cake", "Bake"/"Baked", "Restaurant", "tasting", "baked", as well as related labels like "Professional", "Advanced", "molecular". This pattern appears repeatedly across layers 13–25 and positions 0–4.
- Norm heatmap: the difference magnitude is small in early layers and then grows sharply in middle-to-late layers, peaking around layers 20–25, and is largest at the earliest token positions (pos0–pos2). That localization (deep layers + early positions) is consistent with a semantic/next-token preference rather than a low-level formatting change.
- The sign of the decode (these are B − A logit-lens directions) implies B is more “pulled toward” culinary tokens than A — i.e., B would be more likely to continue with food/cooking/baking content in situations captured by these residual directions.

Caveats
- I cannot identify the exact training intervention (e.g., recipe-finetuning, domain-adaptation on food blogs, or some other data mix) from this evidence alone — only that the observable effect is a culinary-domain bias.
- Patchscope continuations were not supplied here (or did not appear in the report), so I can’t show behavioral continuations to corroborate the logit-lens signal; the logit-lens + norm pattern is already strong evidence, however.
